summary: Changes the type codes and mnemonics of the DNSSEC records SIG, KEY and NXT to avoid dangerous interactions between older resolvers and servers that understand the new delegation signer semantics. One failure case made an unsecured zone unresolvable. It updates RFC 2535 and RFC 3658, and was replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

eli5.summary: Old and new versions of a secret-signing system confused each other. This gave the new pieces fresh names so old computers would ignore them.

questions: why were dnssec sig key nxt records renamed
what is the difference between nxt and nsec
what are the dnssec rrsig nsec and dnskey type codes
subtitle: How DNSSEC got new record types so old resolvers would stop hiding unsigned delegations.

tldr.problem: Servers that understand the Delegation Signer (DS) semantics return NXT records in referrals to unsecure delegations. Some deployed RFC 2535 resolvers read any NXT as proof that a name does not exist, so those delegations become unresolvable.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives the DNSSEC records new type codes and names: RRSIG replaces SIG, DNSKEY replaces KEY and NSEC replaces NXT. Legacy resolvers then treat them as unknown records and ignore them.
tldr.outcome: Signing zones with DS no longer risks hiding unsecured delegations from legacy resolvers. The RFC itself was later replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

today: RFC 3755 is a Proposed Standard that has been replaced by RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035. It was also updated by RFC 3757 and RFC 3845, and it updated RFC 2535 and RFC 3658.

sections.title: The Compatibility Problem
sections.content:
DNSSEC went through several iterations whose syntax and semantics are not fully compatible, and earlier DNS specifications said little about how resolvers should behave. The result is fielded code with a wide variety of behaviors, which makes the effect of any protocol change hard to predict. One way to manage the risk is to structure changes so that existing resolvers can completely ignore input that might confuse them.

The specific trigger is the Delegation Signer (DS) of RFC 3658. In RFC 2535, NXT records only had to be returned as part of a proof that a name does not exist. With DS, a referral to an unsecure delegation also carries an NXT and its signature, proving that no DS record exists. RFC 2535 did not say how to read a response with RCODE=0, AA=0 and both an NS and an NXT in the authority section.

Some widely deployed RFC 2535 resolvers treat any answer containing an NXT as a proof of non-existence. Unsecure delegations then become invisible to them, which breaks the principle that DNSSEC must do no harm: signing a zone must not stop unsecured delegations from resolving.
sections.eli5: Imagine a note that used to mean only "nothing here." Then a new note with the same label started meaning "nothing signed here, but keep looking." Old readers saw the label and stopped looking.

sections.title: Solutions Considered
sections.content:
The RFC weighs five options. Change the SIG, KEY and NXT type codes is the simplest and has been tested most. Its cost is that new resolvers cannot validate zones signed with the old records, but that problem already exists because of DS, and legacy resolvers are far more common than zones signed under RFC 2535.

Changing only a subset of the codes looks simpler but may miss other incompatibilities, and legacy resolvers could be confused by recognizing SIG and KEY while finding no NXT. Replacing the DO bit with a new EDNS0 flag (tentatively called DA) works only if every RFC 2535 resolver zeroes unknown flags, which cannot be assumed. Incrementing the EDNS version relies on old implementations rejecting higher versions, and had not been tested.

Doing nothing would leave zone owners with a strong reason not to sign zones that contain unsecure delegations, and would slow DNSSEC adoption, since resolver operators have no incentive to upgrade without signed zones.
sections.eli5: They tried to think of several ways to stop old computers from getting confused. Renaming the pieces was the cleanest, because everyone already knows what happens when a computer sees a name it does not know: it skips it.

sections.title: The New Record Types
sections.content:
The chosen solution gives the three records new type codes and new mnemonics. DNSKEY replaces KEY (the name signals these keys are not for application use, per RFC 3445), RRSIG replaces SIG, and NSEC replaces NXT. SIG(0) and TKEY keep using SIG and KEY.

The new types have exactly the syntax and semantics of the old ones in RFC 2535 and RFC 3658, with three exceptions. Domain names embedded in RRSIG and NSEC MUST NOT be compressed. Embedded names are not downcased for DNSSEC canonical form, ordering or equality comparison. An RRSIG whose type-covered field is zero has undefined semantics, which only an IETF Standards Action may define.

A resolver that receives the old types SHOULD treat them as unknown records and MUST NOT use them for DNSSEC validation. For example, it must not use a DNSKEY to validate a SIG or a KEY to validate an RRSIG. The RFC also clarifies that some positive responses, such as wildcard proofs and unsecure referrals, contain NSEC records, and resolvers MUST NOT treat an answer as negative merely because it contains one.
sections.eli5: The old names were retired for this job and new names took over. A computer that only knows the old names sees the new ones as strangers and leaves them alone.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content:
The DNS resource record type registry assigns types 46, 47 and 48 to RRSIG, NSEC and DNSKEY. Types 24 and 25 (SIG and KEY) stay for SIG(0) and TKEY, and type 30 (NXT) is marked Obsolete.

The DNS Security Algorithm Numbers registry gains two columns showing whether each algorithm may be used for zone signing, transaction security, or both. Only RSA/SHA-1, DSA/SHA-1 and the private algorithms (types 253 and 254) may be used for zone signing. The RFC assigns RSA/SHA-1 the mnemonic RSASHA1.

A new registry is created for the DNSKEY flags field, initially holding only bit 7, the ZONE bit. The DNSKEY protocol octet has a single defined value, 3 (DNSSEC), so it needs no registry.
sections.eli5: The official list of record names gets three new entries, and the old ones are either kept for other jobs or marked as retired.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says the changes do not materially affect security. Mixing new and legacy types is not well understood and would probably lead to unintended and dangerous results. Changing type codes also leaves code paths in legacy resolvers that are never exercised, and unexercised code is a frequent source of security holes. Doing nothing would slow DNSSEC deployment, which does not reduce security but does not improve it either.
sections.eli5: Do not mix old and new names. Old code that never gets used is a place where bugs can hide.
